9.text: The Chukchee are well aware of the extreme nervousness of their shamans,

10.text: and express it by the word nɪñɪˊrkɪlqin (“he is bashful”). By this word they

11.text: mean to convey the idea that the shaman is highly sensitive even to the

12.text: slightest change of the psychic atmosphere surrounding him during his exer-

13.text: cises. For instance, the Chukchee shaman is diffident in acting before strangers,

14.text: especially shortly after his initiation. A shaman of great power will refuse

15.text: to show his skill when among strangers, and will yield only after much soli-

16.text: citation: even then, as a rule, he will not show all of his power. He is shy

17.text: of strange people, of a house to which he is unaccustomed, of “alien” drums

18.text: and charms which are hidden in their bags, and of “spirits” that hover around.

19.text: The least doubt or sneer makes him break off the performance and retire.

20.text: The shamanistic “spirits” are likewise described as “fleeting” (nɪrɪˊnᴀqên),

21.text: meaning that they want to flee before every unusual face or voice. When

22.text: too many strange visitors come to the shaman, the “spirits” are shy of ap-

23.text: pearing, and, even when they do come, they are all the time anxious to slip

24.text: away. Once when I induced a shaman to practise at my house, his “spirits”

25.text: (of a ventriloquistic kind) for a long time refused to come. When at last

26.text: they did come, they were heard walking around the house outside and

27.text: knocking on its walls, as if still undecided whether to enter. When they

30.text: “Keˊlet belong to the wilderness,” say the shamans, “just as much as

31.text: any wild animal. This is the reason that they are so fleeting.” Keˊlet of

32.text: the animal kind have this shyness to an extreme degree. When coming at

33.text: the call of the shaman, they sniff and snort, and finally, after some short

34.text: exercise on the drum, flee back to the freedom of the wilderness. All this,
